query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by the formation of a stable, coherent oxide layer on the surface, which acts as a barrier to abrasive wear and reduces the coefficient of friction.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, polycrystalline high-entropy alloy coating with a composition of FeCoCrNiMn
generation.intervention: Annealing at 800°C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere
generation.conditions: Dry sliding wear test with a normal load of 10 N and a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s
generation.mechanism: Formation of a stable oxide layer reduces abrasive wear by preventing direct metal-to-metal contact and reducing the coefficient of friction
generation.predicted_outcome: A 30% reduction in wear rate compared to the as-deposited coating, measured in terms of volume loss per unit distance (mm³/m)
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for high-entropy alloy coatings with a composition range of FeCoCrNiMn and annealing temperatures between 700°C and 900°C
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and microstructure of the oxide layer, as well as the potential for other wear mechanisms to contribute to the overall wear performance

falsification_experiment.design: Dry sliding wear test with a normal load of 10 N and a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate of the annealed coating is not reduced by at least 20% compared to the as-deposited coating, the hypothesis is falsified
